questions.title: Referred pain of appendicitis
questions.question: Regarding the large intestine, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Pain of appendicitis is usually referred to the region of the umbilicus
options.B: The left colic flexure lies in front of the right kidney
options.C: Appendices epiploicae are present in the appendix and caecum
options.D: The appendix mostly lies in the subcaecal position (75%)

explanations.A: Correct. Early appendicular pain is visceral, carried by sympathetic afferents that accompany the midgut to the T10 spinal segment, so it is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus. Only later, when the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum, does the pain shift and localise to McBurney's point in the right iliac fossa. This visceral-to-somatic migration of pain is a classic diagnostic feature of appendicitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left colic (splenic) flexure lies in front of the left kidney; it is the right colic (hepatic) flexure that relates to the right kidney.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Appendices epiploicae are fat-filled peritoneal tags characteristic of the colon; they are absent on the appendix and the caecum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The appendix most often lies in the retrocaecal/retrocolic position (about 65-75%); the subcaecal position is uncommon.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the periumbilical referral of early appendicitis pain from the midgut.

questions.title: Ureter crossing the common iliac bifurcation
questions.question: Regarding the ureter, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Pain sensation is carried from the ureter to the upper two thoracic and upper two lumbar segments of the spinal cord
options.B: The inferior vena cava lies lateral to the right ureter
options.C: While lying on the psoas major it is crossed anteriorly by the genitofemoral nerve
options.D: It crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ureteric pain is referred to the T11-L2 segments (loin to groin), not the upper two thoracic segments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava lies medial to the right ureter, not lateral to it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. On the psoas major the ureter is crossed anteriorly by the gonadal (testicular/ovarian) vessels; the genitofemoral nerve lies behind it, on the surface of the muscle.
explanations.D: Correct. The abdominal ureter descends on the psoas major and enters the pelvis by crossing in front of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim, over the sacroiliac joint. This crossing is a key surgical landmark used to identify the ureter. It is also one of the three normal sites of ureteric narrowing where calculi tend to impact.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the ureter as it crosses the common iliac bifurcation at the pelvic brim.

questions.title: Inferior mesenteric artery territory
questions.question: Regarding the blood supply of the gut, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The splenic artery lies deep to the body of the pancreas
options.B: The superior mesenteric vein lies on the left side of the superior mesenteric artery
options.C: The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery
options.D: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the left one-third of the transverse colon

explanations.A: Incorrect. The splenic artery runs a tortuous course along the superior border of the body of the pancreas, not deep to it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior mesenteric vein lies on the right side of the superior mesenteric artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a branch of the gastroduodenal artery (from the coeliac trunk); only the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery comes from the SMA.
explanations.D: Correct. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut: the distal (left) third of the transverse colon, the descending and sigmoid colon and the upper rectum, through its left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal branches. The boundary with the SMA territory near the splenic flexure is the watershed zone of Griffiths, vulnerable to ischaemia. The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon remain SMA (midgut) territory.

questions.learning_objective: Define the colonic territory of the inferior mesenteric artery and the splenic-flexure watershed.

questions.title: Superior mesenteric vessels and the uncinate process
questions.question: Regarding the pancreas, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The tail passes through the gastrosplenic ligament
options.B: The superior mesenteric vessels lie anterior to the uncinate process of the head
options.C: The left renal vein lies anterior to the body
options.D: The pyloroduodenal junction lies behind the neck

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum of the spleen within the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament, not the gastrosplenic ligament.
explanations.B: Correct. The uncinate process is the hook-like inferior projection of the head of the pancreas that passes behind the superior mesenteric vessels, so the SMA and SMV lie anterior to it. This explains why a carcinoma of the uncinate process can encase these vessels and render the tumour unresectable. The vessels emerge from beneath the neck of the pancreas to cross the third part of the duodenum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left renal vein passes posterior to the body of the pancreas (and anterior to the aorta), not anterior to the body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pyloroduodenal junction lies to the right of the neck, not behind it.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the relation of the uncinate process to the superior mesenteric vessels.

questions.title: Anterior relations of the right kidney
questions.question: Regarding the kidney, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The right kidney is slightly higher than the left kidney
options.B: The second part of the duodenum is related to the anterior surface of the right kidney close to the hilum
options.C: At the hilum, the renal artery lies anterior to the renal vein
options.D: The renal fascia is derived from the fascia iliaca

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left because it is displaced downward by the large right lobe of the liver.
explanations.B: Correct. The descending (second) part of the duodenum passes vertically over the anterior surface of the medial part of the right kidney, close to the hilum and the right renal vessels. This intimate relation is why a posterior duodenal ulcer may erode toward the kidney and its vessels. Anteriorly the second part is also crossed by the transverse colon.
explanations.C: Incorrect. At the hilum the renal vein is the most anterior structure, then the artery, then the pelvis (V-A-P from front to back).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The renal fascia (of Gerota) is condensed extraperitoneal/transversalis fascia, not a derivative of the fascia iliaca.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the second part of the duodenum as an anterior relation of the right kidney.

questions.title: Nerve through the superficial inguinal ring
questions.question: Which of the following nerves passes through the superficial inguinal ring?

options.A: Iliohypogastric nerve
options.B: Obturator nerve
options.C: Ilioinguinal nerve
options.D: Pudendal nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. The iliohypogastric nerve pierces the external oblique aponeurosis about 2 cm above the superficial inguinal ring; it does not pass through the ring.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen to reach the medial thigh and has no relation to the inguinal canal.
explanations.C: Correct. The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) enters the inguinal canal by piercing the internal oblique rather than passing through the deep ring, runs anterior to the spermatic cord, and emerges through the superficial inguinal ring. It supplies the skin of the upper medial thigh and the anterior scrotum or labium majus. It is therefore the nerve at risk during herniorrhaphy at the superficial ring.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pudendal nerve exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen to supply the perineum; it does not traverse the inguinal canal.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the ilioinguinal nerve emerging through the superficial inguinal ring.

questions.title: Formation of the hepatopancreatic ampulla
questions.question: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct join to form the:

options.A: Hepatic duct
options.B: Common hepatic duct
options.C: Cystic duct
options.D: Ampulla of Vater

explanations.A: Incorrect. The (right and left) hepatic ducts drain bile out of the liver lobes and unite to form the common hepatic duct; they lie upstream of the common bile duct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The common hepatic duct is formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts, before the cystic duct joins it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cystic duct connects the gall bladder to the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct; it is not formed by the union in the question.
explanations.D: Correct. The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens at the major duodenal papilla on the posteromedial wall of the second part of the duodenum. The ampulla is encircled by the sphincter of Oddi. A gallstone impacted here obstructs both biliary and pancreatic outflow and can cause gallstone pancreatitis.

questions.learning_objective: Name the structure formed by the union of the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct.

questions.title: Peritoneal connection between liver and stomach
questions.question: Which one of the following forms a connection between the liver and the stomach?

options.A: Lesser omentum
options.B: Greater omentum
options.C: Left triangular ligament of the liver
options.D: Gastrosplenic ligament

explanations.A: Correct. The lesser omentum is a double peritoneal fold that runs from the porta hepatis and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum of the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum. Its two named parts are the hepatogastric and the hepatoduodenal ligaments. Its free right margin transmits the portal triad and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The greater omentum hangs down from the greater curvature of the stomach as an apron over the small intestine; it does not connect liver to stomach.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left triangular ligament connects the left lobe of the liver to the diaphragm, not to the stomach.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the hilum of the spleen.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the lesser omentum as the hepatogastric peritoneal connection.

questions.title: Blood supply of jejunum and ileum
questions.question: The jejunum and ileum receive their blood supply from branches of the:

options.A: Coeliac trunk
options.B: Superior mesenteric artery
options.C: Inferior mesenteric artery
options.D: Gastroduodenal artery

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coeliac trunk supplies foregut derivatives (stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, spleen, pancreas), not the jejunum and ileum.
explanations.B: Correct. The jejunum and ileum are midgut derivatives supplied by the jejunal and ileal branches that arise from the left side of the superior mesenteric artery and form looping arcades in the mesentery. Straight vessels (vasa recta) pass from the arcades to the gut wall. The SMA also supplies the caecum, appendix, ascending colon and the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut (left colon and upper rectum), not the small intestine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The gastroduodenal artery supplies the pylorus, proximal duodenum and part of the pancreas, not the jejunum and ileum.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the arterial supply of the jejunum and ileum to the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.title: Dual blood supply of the duodenum
questions.question: Regarding the duodenum, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The right ureter lies deep to the first part
options.B: The first part lies deep to the caudate lobe of the liver
options.C: The third part lies at the level of L2
options.D: It is supplied by both the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right ureter is related to the second and third parts of the duodenum posteriorly, not deep to the first part.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The first part is related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and the gall bladder anteriorly; the caudate lobe relates to the lesser sac.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third (horizontal) part crosses at the level of L3; it is the whole duodenum that runs from L1 to L2 overall, with the flexure at L2.
explanations.D: Correct. The duodenum straddles the foregut-midgut junction at the level of the major duodenal papilla, so it has a dual blood supply. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, from the gastroduodenal branch of the coeliac trunk, supplies the part proximal to the papilla, while the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the SMA supplies the distal part, the two anastomosing in the pancreaticoduodenal arcade.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the dual coeliac and superior mesenteric supply of the duodenum at the embryological junction.

questions.title: Inferior epigastric artery at the deep ring
questions.question: Regarding the anterior abdominal wall, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The inferior epigastric artery ascends on the medial side of the deep inguinal ring
options.B: The ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves pierce the rectus abdominis muscle
options.C: The upper part of the rectus abdominis muscle rests directly on the fascia transversalis
options.D: The tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis are connected to the posterior wall of the rectus sheath

explanations.A: Correct. The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament and ascends on the medial side of the deep inguinal ring, raising the lateral umbilical fold before entering the rectus sheath. It therefore lies medial to the neck of an indirect inguinal hernia and lateral to a direct hernia, distinguishing the two. Surgeons ligate this vessel to reduce a hernia at the deep ring.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves run in the neurovascular plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis; they do not pierce the rectus abdominis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Above the costal margin the rectus abdominis rests on the 5th-7th costal cartilages, and lower down on the posterior rectus sheath and fascia transversalis; it does not rest directly on fascia transversalis in its upper part.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The tendinous intersections adhere firmly to the anterior wall of the rectus sheath, not the posterior wall, which is why they produce the surface furrows of the 'six-pack'.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the inferior epigastric artery medial to the deep inguinal ring and its hernia significance.

questions.title: Attachments of the inguinal ligament
questions.question: Regarding the inguinal ligament, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: It is attached laterally to the anterior superior iliac spine
options.B: The lacunar ligament extends from the lateral part of the inguinal ligament to the pectineal line
options.C: It is attached medially to the pubic crest
options.D: It is the lower free border of the internal oblique aponeurosis

explanations.A: Correct. The inguinal ligament is the rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis and stretches from the anterior superior iliac spine laterally to the pubic tubercle medially. It forms the floor of the inguinal canal. Its medial fibres extend backward and laterally as the lacunar ligament to reach the pecten pubis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lacunar ligament extends from the MEDIAL end of the inguinal ligament (near the pubic tubercle) to the pecten pubis, forming the sharp medial border of the femoral ring.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inguinal ligament is attached medially to the pubic tubercle, not the pubic crest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the lower free border of the EXTERNAL oblique aponeurosis, not the internal oblique.

questions.learning_objective: State the bony attachments of the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle).

questions.title: Origin of the short gastric arteries
questions.question: Considering the short gastric arteries, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: They supply the lesser curvature of the stomach
options.B: They reach the stomach through the lienorenal ligament
options.C: They are branches of the splenic artery
options.D: They pass between the two layers of the greater omentum

explanations.A: Incorrect. The short gastric arteries supply the fundus of the stomach, not the lesser curvature, which is supplied by the left and right gastric arteries.
explanations.B: Incorrect. They reach the stomach through the gastrosplenic ligament, not the lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament, which transmits the splenic vessels and tail of pancreas.
explanations.C: Correct. The short gastric arteries (vasa brevia) are four to six small vessels arising from the splenic artery or its terminal branches near the hilum of the spleen. They run in the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus of the stomach and anastomose with the left gastric and left gastro-omental arteries. Because they are short and fragile they are readily torn during splenectomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. They run within the gastrosplenic ligament, not between the two layers of the greater omentum.

questions.learning_objective: Trace the short gastric arteries from the splenic artery to the gastric fundus.

questions.title: Termination of the sigmoid colon
questions.question: The sigmoid (pelvic) colon terminates at the level of the:

options.A: First sacral piece
options.B: Second sacral piece
options.C: Third sacral piece
options.D: Fourth sacral piece

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sigmoid colon begins at the pelvic brim, roughly at the first sacral level, but that is where it starts, not where it ends.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The second sacral level marks the lower limit of the peritoneal cavity behind the rectum, not the rectosigmoid junction.
explanations.C: Correct. The sigmoid colon continues from the descending colon at the pelvic brim and ends by becoming the rectum in front of the third piece of the sacrum (S3). The rectosigmoid junction at S3 is where the sigmoid mesocolon disappears and the taeniae coli fan out into a continuous longitudinal muscle coat. This level is an important landmark during sigmoidoscopy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fourth sacral level relates to the middle of the rectum, below the rectosigmoid junction.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sigmoid colon becomes the rectum at the level of S3.

questions.title: The conjoint tendon
questions.question: Regarding the conjoint tendon, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: It lies in the medial half of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal
options.B: It is controlled by the iliohypogastric nerve
options.C: It lies posterior to the lower part of the rectus sheath
options.D: It is formed by the fused arched fibres of the external oblique and transversus abdominis muscles

explanations.A: Correct. The conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) is formed by the fused aponeurotic fibres of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, which arch over the spermatic cord to attach to the pubic crest and pecten pubis. It reinforces the medial half of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, directly behind the superficial ring. Weakness of this reinforcement at that site predisposes to a direct inguinal hernia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The conjoint tendon is an aponeurotic tendon, not a contractile structure under nerve control; the muscles that form it are supplied by the lower thoracic and L1 nerves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The conjoint tendon lies anterior to the lower part of the rectus sheath, blending with it, not posterior to it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is formed by the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, not the external oblique.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the conjoint tendon reinforcing the medial posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

questions.title: Branches of the abdominal aorta (untrue statement)
questions.question: Regarding the branches of the abdominal aorta, which one of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.A: It gives three pairs of lumbar arteries
options.B: Its testicular branch passes through the inguinal canal
options.C: Its inferior mesenteric branch arises from its ventral aspect
options.D: Its median sacral branch arises from its dorsal aspect

explanations.A: Correct (this is the untrue statement). The abdominal aorta usually gives FOUR pairs of lumbar arteries from its posterolateral surface, not three, to supply the posterior abdominal wall and spinal cord. Because the question asks which statement is not correct, this is the answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The testicular artery arises from the aorta and passes through the inguinal canal within the spermatic cord to reach the testis.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The inferior mesenteric artery, a ventral (anterior) visceral branch, arises from the front of the aorta at about L3.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The median sacral artery arises from the back (dorsal aspect) of the aorta just above its bifurcation.

questions.learning_objective: Recall that the abdominal aorta gives four pairs of lumbar arteries.

questions.title: Vein outside the portal system
questions.question: One of the following veins does NOT belong to the portal system:

options.A: Superior rectal vein
options.B: Superior mesenteric vein
options.C: Left suprarenal vein
options.D: Splenic vein

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer. The superior rectal vein drains via the inferior mesenteric vein into the portal system and is a site of portosystemic anastomosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer. The superior mesenteric vein is one of the two main tributaries that unite behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.
explanations.C: Correct (the odd one out). The left suprarenal (adrenal) vein drains into the left renal vein and thence to the inferior vena cava, so it belongs to the systemic (caval) venous system, not the portal system. By contrast the superior rectal, superior mesenteric and splenic veins are all tributaries of the hepatic portal vein. The left suprarenal vein is therefore the systemic exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer. The splenic vein unites with the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein and receives the inferior mesenteric vein.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish systemic tributaries such as the suprarenal vein from portal tributaries.

questions.title: Blood supply of the liver (untrue statement)
questions.question: Regarding the liver, which one of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.A: The bare area is on the posterior surface of the right lobe
options.B: The hepatic artery supplies about 70% of the total blood entering the liver
options.C: In the upper part of the groove for the inferior vena cava there are openings for the exit of the hepatic veins
options.D: The caudate and quadrate lobes receive blood from the left branch of the hepatic artery

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The bare area is a triangular region on the posterior surface of the right lobe, in direct contact with the diaphragm and devoid of peritoneum.
explanations.B: Correct (this is the untrue statement). The hepatic artery provides only about 25-30% of the blood entering the liver (though roughly half of its oxygen); the hepatic PORTAL VEIN supplies the remaining 70-75%. Because the question asks for the statement that is not correct, this is the answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The hepatic veins leave the liver in the upper part of the groove for the inferior vena cava to drain into it.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer (the statement is true). The caudate and quadrate lobes are functionally part of the left lobe and are supplied by the left branch of the hepatic artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the portal vein, not the hepatic artery, supplies most of the liver's blood inflow.

questions.title: Arterial supply of the testis
questions.question: Regarding the testis, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: It receives its arterial supply from the abdominal aorta
options.B: Its venous drainage ends on both sides in the renal veins
options.C: It has lymphatic drainage to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes
options.D: It is in the scrotum by the fifth month of intra-uterine life

explanations.A: Correct. The testicular (gonadal) artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries, reflecting the high embryological origin of the testis on the posterior abdominal wall. It descends retroperitoneally and enters the spermatic cord to reach the testis. This high origin also explains the para-aortic lymphatic drainage of the organ.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava while the left drains into the left renal vein; they do not both end in the renal veins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Testicular lymph drains to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at the level of L1-L2, following the artery; only the scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The testis normally descends into the scrotum by about the seventh to ninth month of intra-uterine life, not the fifth month.

questions.module_subject: 206 DIG > Anatomy > Testis and spermatic cord
questions.learning_objective: Trace the testicular artery from the abdominal aorta and relate it to lymphatic drainage.

questions.title: Vertebral levels of the duodenum
questions.question: Regarding the duodenum, choose the correct statement:

options.A: It develops from the midgut and hindgut
options.B: The second part is related to the hilum of the left kidney
options.C: It begins at the level of L1 and ends at the level of L2
options.D: It is completely covered by peritoneum

explanations.A: Incorrect. The duodenum develops from the caudal foregut and the cranial midgut, the junction lying at the major duodenal papilla; the hindgut has no part in it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The second part descends over the hilum of the RIGHT kidney, not the left.
explanations.C: Correct. The duodenum begins at the pylorus at the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and ends at the duodenojejunal flexure at the level of L2, forming a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas. Only the first 2 cm (the duodenal cap) is intraperitoneal and mobile; the rest is secondarily retroperitoneal. The duodenojejunal flexure is suspended by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Most of the duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal and covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface only; just the proximal cap is completely peritonealised.

questions.learning_objective: State that the duodenum extends from L1 to L2 and is largely retroperitoneal.
